paras: The burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm took place near Cardington, Ohio, on the night of June 5, 1882, when a mob burned the house, barn and farm buildings of Archer, a Black man, while he was held in jail for shooting three people. The sheriff kept Archer from a crowd that had threatened to lynch him, and the story circulated in Ohio and beyond because the quarrel was said to have begun with neighbors refusing to call him "Mister Archer."

According to a Mount Gilead dispatch to the Cincinnati Enquirer, Archer, a "colored citizen of Cardington," had for many years been on bad terms with many of his townsmen because they would not call him Mr. Archer. A New York Sun paragraph said people addressed him familiarly as "Tom" and that Archer, described as "half negro," took this as "a studied insult because of his color."

A wire brief reported that on June 5 Archer "attempted to drive over" A. Sherman and T. Payne at Cardington, and that when they objected he fired a shotgun, hitting both men and a boy. An earlier wire item described a quarrel on the Bee line road in which Archer fired on two men, named as Sherman and Hayneworth, and said a mob was organizing.

Archer was arrested, and the Mount Gilead correspondent wrote that a mob was raised and that "some of the leading citizens" made threats of lynching. The sheriff and his deputy were called from Mount Gilead and the Levering Guards were held ready, while the sheriff hid his prisoner for about two hours before lodging him in the Mount Gilead jail at midnight. At about eleven o'clock that night a fire was seen toward Cardington, and the correspondent later learned that Archer's house, barn and farm buildings had been burned "by the excited mob."
No report of an arrest for the burning, of a trial of Archer, or of the condition of the wounded was found in the coverage.

The first notice, a one-sentence wire item in the St. Paul Daily Globe on June 7, predicted that Archer would be lynched if any of the wounded died. A longer wire brief ran in the Huntsville Gazette on June 10 and the Iron County Register on June 15, and the same day the "Ohio State News" column in the Somerset Press and the Eaton Democrat told of the burning, calling the burners "troubled people" and "outraged people" respectively.

Papers built the story around the dispute over a title: the Mount Gilead dispatch was reprinted in Montana in July under the headline "He Wanted to be Called Mr.," and the Yorkville Enquirer in South Carolina said "the whole difficulty" grew out of Archer's anger at being refused "Mr." The New York Sun's version, reprinted in the Arkansaw Traveler and the Lake Charles Commercial, said none of the three was much hurt and that the mob burned his farm after failing to lynch him. The Perrysburg Journal called the affair "a first class sensation" and, alone among the papers, said Archer "has a bad reputation, and was always armed."

Accounts differed on whether a lynching was actually attempted: the Perrysburg Journal said an attempt was made while he was being taken to jail, while the Mount Gilead correspondent described only threats and called the crowd at the jail "perfectly harmless." Reports of the wounded also varied, from two men expected to die in the first wire item, to two men and a boy seriously hurt, to three people none of whom was "much hurt."

reader.title: Burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm, Cardington, Ohio
bases: After Archer's arrest a mob threatened or tried to lynch him and, while he was in jail, burned his house, barn and farm buildings (A5, A8, A9).

A Mt. Gilead dispatch (A9), the Ohio State News column (A5) and a separate wire brief (A3) independently report the shooting and the lynching threats, and A5, A8 and A9 report the burning of his farm buildings.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Archer tried to drive over Sherman and Payne; when they objected he shot them and a boy, was arrested, and a crowd threatened to lynch him.

accounts.label: Mt. Gilead correspondent (Cincinnati Enquirer)
accounts.gist: A long quarrel over the title 'Mr.' ended with Archer shooting three; leading citizens threatened lynching, the sheriff hid and jailed him, and an 'excited mob' burned his farm buildings.

accounts.label: Perrysburg Journal
accounts.gist: An attempt to lynch Archer on the way to jail failed and the people then burned his house, barn and outhouses; the paper adds that he had a bad reputation and was always armed.

framing.detail: Ohio papers ran it as a brief in the 'Ohio State News' column, one calling the burners 'troubled people' and another 'outraged people'.
The Perrysburg Journal called it 'a first class sensation' and blamed Archer's 'bad reputation'.
The New York Sun paragraph, reprinted in Arkansas and Louisiana, explained Archer's anger as resentment of 'a studied insult because of his color'.
The Mt. Gilead dispatch, headed 'He Wanted to be Called Mr.', called the jail crowd 'perfectly harmless' yet said 'the excited mob' burned his buildings.
